title: The Full English Breakfast
blurb: The undisputed king of breakfasts — back bacon, butcher’s sausages, eggs, beans, black pudding, grilled tomato and fried bread, all cooked in one pan wherever possible.
ingredients: 2 slices white bread, fried in dripping
1 tbsp beef dripping or vegetable oil
Butter, brown sauce and tea, to serve
steps: Warm a large frying pan over a medium heat with half the dripping. Add the sausages and cook gently for 12–15 minutes, turning until burnished and cooked through.
Push the sausages to one side. Add the bacon and black pudding; fry 3–4 minutes per side until crisp at the edges. Keep everything warm in a low oven.
Add the tomato halves cut-side down with the mushrooms; season and cook 4 minutes until caramelised.
Meanwhile, warm the beans in a small pan over a low heat, stirring occasionally.
Fry the bread in the bacon fat until golden and crisp. Remove, then crack in the eggs and fry to your liking — sunny-side up is traditional.
Plate everything together: eggs last, beans in a small pot if you’re feeling proper. Brown sauce on the table, tea strong enough to stand a spoon in.

title: Proper Bacon Butty
blurb: Crisp streaky bacon in a soft white bap with a lash of butter — the nation’s favourite handheld breakfast, no garnish required and none wanted.
ingredients: HP brown sauce or ketchup, to taste
steps: Lay the bacon in a cold frying pan and set over a medium heat — starting cold renders the fat and crisps the rashers evenly.
Fry 6–8 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden and crisp at the edges.
Split and butter the baps generously. Pile in the hot bacon.
Sauce as you see fit: brown sauce for tradition, ketchup for the young ones. Eat immediately, ideally with a mug of builder’s tea.

title: Grilled Kippers with Butter
blurb: Oak-smoked Northumberland kippers grilled with a knob of butter — the breakfast of kings on the great Victorian and Edwardian tables.
ingredients: Brown bread and butter, to serve
steps: Heat the grill to high (about 240°C / 465°F). Line the grill pan with foil.
Lay the kippers skin-side up on the foil and dot with half the butter.
Grill 4 minutes, turn carefully, dot with the remaining butter and grill 3–4 minutes more until sizzling.
Alternatively, jug them: stand the kippers head-down in a tall jug, cover with boiling water for 6 minutes, then drain — no smell, perfectly cooked.
Serve with a dusting of cayenne, lemon wedges and thick brown bread and butter.

title: Black Pudding with a Fried Egg
blurb: Thick slices of proper Bury black pudding, fried until crisp-edged and crowned with a runny-yolked egg — a northern breakfast of champions.
ingredients: 4 thick slices Bury black pudding, about 2cm
2 slices thick-cut sourdough or white toast
steps: Heat the dripping in a frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Fry the black pudding slices 3–4 minutes per side — you want a crisp crust and a soft, yielding middle.
Toast and butter the bread while the pudding cooks.
In the same pan, fry the eggs until the whites are set and lacy and the yolks still run.
Slide the black pudding onto the toast, crown with the egg, season well and cut in so the yolk runs into the pudding.

title: Smoked Haddock Kedgeree
blurb: Flaked smoked haddock folded through buttery curried rice with soft eggs and parsley — the great Anglo-Indian breakfast dish of the Raj, still unbeatable on a slow weekend.
steps: Poach the haddock in the milk at a bare simmer for 6–8 minutes until it flakes easily. Lift out, discard the skin and flake into large pieces. Reserve the milk.
Soft-boil the eggs for 6½ minutes, then shell and quarter them.
Cook the rice in boiling salted water until just tender; drain well.
Melt the butter in a wide pan, soften the onion for 8 minutes, then stir in the curry powder and cook 1 minute more.
Tip in the rice with a ladle of the poaching milk; fold together over a low heat until glossy.
Gently fold in the haddock, cream and parsley. Warm through for 2 minutes without breaking up the fish.
Top with the quartered eggs, a twist of black pepper and lemon wedges on the side.

title: Proper Porridge with Honey
blurb: Slow-cooked pinhead oatmeal porridge, creamy and rib-sticking, finished with good English honey and a splash of cold milk.
ingredients: 600ml whole milk (or half milk, half water)
Cold milk or cream, to finish
steps: Tip the oats, milk and salt into a heavy-based pan and bring slowly to a gentle simmer.
Cook over the lowest heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring often, until the oats are swollen and the porridge falls softly from the spoon.
Rest off the heat for 2 minutes — it will thicken to the perfect consistency.
Ladle into warm bowls, drizzle generously with honey and pour round a moat of cold milk or cream.

title: Bubble and Squeak
blurb: Yesterday’s roast potatoes and cabbage fried into a golden, crisp-edged cake — named for the sound it makes in the pan, and the best reason ever to cook too much on Sunday.
ingredients: Salt and plenty of black pepper
steps: If using onion, soften it in half the dripping over a medium heat for 5 minutes.
Mix the cold potato and cabbage with plenty of seasoning — rough is fine; a few lumps are welcome.
Heat the remaining dripping in a heavy frying pan. Press in the potato mixture into an even cake about 3cm thick.
Cook over a medium heat for 8–10 minutes until a deep golden crust forms underneath. Resist moving it.
Invert onto a plate, slide back in crust-side up and cook 8 minutes more until crisp and piping hot.
Serve in wedges, crowned with a fried egg if it’s breakfast, or beside cold meats and pickles if it’s supper.

title: Crumpets with Salted Butter
blurb: Hot toasted crumpets riddled with holes, drowned in salted butter that runs straight through — best eaten leaning over the plate.
steps: Whisk the flour, sugar, yeast and warm milk to a smooth batter. Cover and leave somewhere warm for 1 hour until frothy and doubled.
Beat the bicarbonate and salt into the batter with 100ml warm water.
Grease crumpet rings (or large metal cookie cutters) and a heavy frying pan. Set over a low-medium heat.
Fill each ring 1cm deep with batter. Cook 6–8 minutes until the surface is set and full of holes.
Remove the rings, flip and cook 1 minute more. Repeat with the remaining batter.
To serve, toast until the bottoms are crisp, then anoint with butter so it pours through the holes. Jam after the butter — never before.

title: Staffordshire Oatcakes
blurb: The Potteries’ own pancake — soft, yeasty oatmeal rounds folded round melted cheese and bacon. An oatcake shop breakfast, recreated at home.
ingredients: Fillings: grated cheddar, bacon rashers, mushrooms
steps: Whisk the oatmeal, flour, yeast, salt, sugar and warm liquid into a thin batter. Cover and rest 45 minutes until bubbling.
Ladle a thin layer into a lightly oiled frying pan, tilting to coat like a crêpe.
Cook 2–3 minutes per side until golden freckles appear. Keep warm in a tea towel.
Fill with grated cheese and crisp bacon, fold in half and return to the pan briefly to melt the cheese.
Serve immediately — oatcakes wait for no one.

title: Roast Beef & Yorkshire Pudding
blurb: The dish that built an empire: rose-pink sirloin with crackling-hot Yorkshires, roasties cooked in dripping, and gravy made in the roasting tin. England’s national dish and the most searched Sunday dinner in Britain.
ingredients: 1.8kg beef sirloin or rib joint, on the bone if possible
For the Yorkshires: 140g plain flour, 4 eggs, 200ml milk, pinch of salt
1.5kg Maris Piper potatoes, peeled and chunked
2 onions, halved; 1 carrot; 1 tbsp flour and 500ml beef stock for the gravy
Horseradish sauce and seasonal greens, to serve
steps: Take the beef out of the fridge 1 hour before cooking. Heat the oven to 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7).
Rub the joint with dripping, mustard powder, salt and pepper. Sit it on the onion and carrot in a roasting tin.
Roast 20 minutes at 220°C / 425°F, then turn down to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) and roast 15 minutes per 450g for rare, 20 for medium.
Meanwhile whisk the Yorkshire batter — flour, eggs, milk, salt — until smooth and rest it at room temperature.
Parboil the potatoes 8 minutes, drain and rough them up in the colander. Roast in hot dripping on a tray for 50–60 minutes, turning once.
Rest the beef under foil for at least 30 minutes — this is non-negotiable.
Heat a thin film of dripping in each Yorkshire tin hole until smoking. Pour in the batter and bake at 220°C / 425°F for 18–20 minutes. Do not open the door.
Make the gravy in the roasting tin: stir the flour into the pan juices, cook 1 minute, then whisk in the stock and simmer until glossy.
Carve the beef thickly, serve with puffed Yorkshires, roasties, greens and horseradish.

title: Roast Chicken with Bread Sauce
blurb: A properly roasted free-range bird with burnished skin, served with medieval England’s greatest gift to the dinner table — clove-and-onion bread sauce.
ingredients: For the bread sauce: 500ml milk, 1 onion studded with 6 cloves, 2 bay leaves
Roast potatoes and game chips, to serve
steps: Heat the oven to 190°C / 375°F (fan 170°C, gas 5).
Stuff the cavity with lemon, thyme and garlic. Smear the bird all over with butter and season generously.
Roast for 1 hour 20 minutes, basting twice, until the skin is deep gold and the leg juices run clear (75°C / 167°F at the thigh).
Meanwhile, infuse the milk with the clove-studded onion and bay at a bare simmer for 20 minutes. Discard the onion and bay.
Stir the breadcrumbs into the hot milk; simmer 3 minutes until thick. Finish with butter, cream, salt and white pepper.
Rest the chicken 15 minutes. Carve and serve with the warm bread sauce, roasties and watercress.

title: Roast Leg of Lamb with Mint Sauce
blurb: Studded with garlic and rosemary, roasted to a blush, and cut with sharp, sweet home-made mint sauce — Easter’s essential centrepiece.
ingredients: For the mint sauce: large bunch mint, 2 tbsp caster sugar, 4 tbsp white wine vinegar, 4 tbsp boiling water
500ml lamb or chicken stock and 1 tbsp redcurrant jelly for the gravy
Roast potatoes and spring vegetables, to serve
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6).
Stab the lamb all over and push slivers of garlic and rosemary into the slits. Rub with oil, salt and pepper.
Roast 20 minutes at 200°C / 400°F, then reduce to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) and cook 20 minutes per 500g for pink, 25 for well done.
While it roasts, chop the mint finely, dissolve the sugar in the vinegar and boiling water, and combine. Rest 30 minutes.
Rest the lamb under foil for 20 minutes. Deglaze the tin with the stock and redcurrant jelly for the gravy.
Carve against the grain and serve with the mint sauce at the table, never in the kitchen.

title: Roast Pork with Crackling & Apple Sauce
blurb: Shattering, bubbled crackling over sweet slow-roasted shoulder, with a sharp Bramley apple sauce to cut the richness. The trick is dry skin, salt, and courage.
ingredients: 2kg pork shoulder or loin, skin scored
For the apple sauce: 3 Bramley apples, 25g butter, 1 tbsp sugar, splash of water
Gravy: 1 tbsp flour, 300ml cider, 300ml chicken stock
steps: The night before, dry the skin thoroughly and leave uncovered in the fridge — dry skin is the whole secret of crackling.
Heat the oven to 240°C / 475°F (fan 220°C, gas 9). Rub the skin with oil, salt and fennel seeds, pushing salt into the scores.
Roast 30 minutes at full heat until the skin blisters, then reduce to 170°C / 340°F (fan 150°C, gas 3) and roast 2 hours more.
Meanwhile simmer the apples with butter, sugar and a splash of water for 10 minutes; beat to a fluffy purée.
Rest the pork 20 minutes. Make the gravy with the flour, cider and stock in the roasting tin.
Crack off the crackling in slabs, carve the meat, and serve with apple sauce and as much gravy as decency allows.

title: Honey-Glazed Gammon
blurb: Gently simmered gammon finished in the oven with a sticky honey, mustard and clove glaze — glorious hot on Boxing Day and even better cold from the fridge.
ingredients: 1 onion, 2 carrots, 2 bay leaves, 10 black peppercorns
For the glaze: 4 tbsp honey, 2 tbsp English mustard, 2 tbsp demerara sugar
steps: Soak the gammon in cold water for a few hours if your butcher advises it, then drain.
Cover with fresh water, add the vegetables and spices, and simmer gently for 20 minutes per 500g (about 1 hour 40 minutes).
Heat the oven to 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6).
Strip off the rind, leaving a layer of fat. Score the fat in diamonds and stud each diamond with a clove.
Brush with honey, mustard and sugar. Roast 25–30 minutes until the glaze is burnished and bubbling.
Rest 15 minutes, carve into thick slices, and serve with parsley sauce — or let it go completely cold for the best sandwiches of the year.

title: Roast Goose with Sage & Onion Stuffing
blurb: Before turkey there was goose — burnished, rich and generous, with its own lake of precious fat for the best roast potatoes you will ever eat.
ingredients: For the stuffing: 2 onions sweated in butter, 200g breadcrumbs, 2 tbsp chopped sage, 1 egg, 100g sausagemeat
300ml chicken stock and a splash of port for the gravy
Plain flour for the gravy, 1 tbsp
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7). Prick the goose’s skin all over with a skewer, avoiding the flesh, and season inside and out.
Mix the stuffing ingredients and fill the neck cavity; put the orange and bay in the body cavity.
Sit the goose on a rack in a deep roasting tin. Roast 30 minutes at 220°C / 425°F, then reduce to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4).
Roast 30 minutes per kilo more (about 2 hours), draining off the fat every 40 minutes — save every drop for roast potatoes.
The goose is done when the leg juices run clear. Rest 30 minutes under foil.
Make gravy with the flour, stock and port in the tin. Carve and serve with apple sauce and the sage and onion stuffing.

title: Toad in the Hole
blurb: Butcher’s sausages sunk into a smoking-hot Yorkshire batter that rises in golden crags around them — served only ever with a lake of onion gravy.
ingredients: Onion gravy: 2 sliced onions, 25g butter, 1 tbsp flour, 400ml beef stock, 1 tsp balsamic vinegar
steps: Whisk the flour, eggs, milk and salt to a smooth batter and rest for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7). Put the dripping and sausages in a roasting tin and heat for 10 minutes until the fat is smoking.
Pour the batter around the sausages and return to the oven immediately. Bake 25–30 minutes — do not open the door early.
Meanwhile soften the onions in butter for 15 minutes until golden. Stir in the flour, then the stock and vinegar; simmer 5 minutes until thickened.
The toad is ready when the batter is puffed, deep golden and crisp. Serve at once with onion gravy and peas.

title: Perfect Yorkshire Puddings
blurb: Four ingredients, three rules: equal volumes, a screaming-hot tin, and never open the door. Crisp-crowned, soft-centred, as they have been since 1737.
ingredients: 8 tsp beef dripping or sunflower oil
steps: Whisk the flour and salt with the eggs to a thick paste, then whisk in the milk gradually until the consistency of single cream. Rest at least 30 minutes — overnight in the fridge is even better.
Heat the oven to 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7).
Put a teaspoon of dripping into each hole of an 8-hole tin and heat for 10 minutes until just smoking.
Fill each hole two-thirds full with batter and bake 18–20 minutes until towering and deep golden.
Serve immediately — a Yorkshire waits for no gravy boat.

title: Beef Wellington
blurb: Fillet of beef wrapped in mushroom duxelles, cured ham and golden puff pastry — the great celebration centrepiece, back on Britain’s most-cooked list for every special occasion.
ingredients: Duxelles: 750g chestnut mushrooms, 50g butter, 1 sprig thyme
Madeira or red wine gravy, to serve
steps: Sear the fillet in smoking-hot oil for 2 minutes per side until browned all over. Brush with mustard and cool completely.
Blitz the mushrooms and fry hard in butter with thyme for 10 minutes until completely dry. Cool.
Lay clingfilm on the worktop, arrange the ham, spread over the duxelles, and roll tightly round the fillet. Chill 30 minutes.
Roll the pastry into a rectangle, unwrap the beef onto it and seal it inside. Chill another 30 minutes — a cold Wellington keeps its shape.
Brush with egg yolk, score lightly, and bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 35–40 minutes for medium-rare (50°C / 122°F in the centre).
Rest 15 minutes, carve into thick slices with a serrated knife, and serve with Madeira gravy.

title: Lancashire Hotpot
blurb: Mill-town fuel turned national treasure: neck of lamb stewed slowly under a crisp golden lid of sliced potatoes, with kidneys for tradition and pickled red cabbage alongside.
ingredients: 800g neck of lamb, cut into chunks
500ml lamb stock; 2 tsp Worcestershire sauce; 1 bay leaf
steps: Heat the oven to 170°C / 340°F (fan 150°C, gas 3).
Brown the lamb and kidneys in batches in a little dripping. Remove, then soften the onions and carrots for 8 minutes.
Stir in the flour, return the meat, and add the stock, Worcestershire sauce and bay. Season well.
Tip into a deep casserole. Overlap the potato slices on top in concentric rings, brush with butter and season.
Cover and bake 1½ hours, then uncover and bake 1 hour more at 200°C / 400°F until the potato lid is golden and crisp.
Serve with pickled red cabbage — the traditional and essential counterpoint.

title: Shepherd’s Pie
blurb: Minced lamb simmered in rich gravy under a furrowed, golden mash — the correct shepherd’s pie is always lamb, and always better the day after.
ingredients: Topping: 1kg floury potatoes, 60g butter, 4 tbsp warm milk, 2 egg yolks
steps: Brown the lamb in batches in a hot pan; drain off most of the fat.
Soften the onions and carrots for 10 minutes. Stir in the tomato purée and flour, cook 2 minutes.
Return the lamb, add the stock, Worcestershire sauce and herbs; simmer 25 minutes until thick and glossy. Stir in the peas.
Boil the potatoes until tender, drain well, and mash with butter, warm milk and yolks until smooth.
Tip the lamb into a baking dish, top with mash and furrow with a fork.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 25–30 minutes until the peaks are golden and the gravy bubbles at the edges.

title: Cottage Pie
blurb: The beefy sibling of the shepherd’s pie — humble cottage cooking from the days when potatoes were the poor man’s roof. Deeply savoury and endlessly comforting.
ingredients: 1 bay leaf; few shakes Worcestershire sauce
Topping: 1kg potatoes, 50g butter, splash of milk, 50g grated cheddar (optional)
steps: Brown the mince hard in a hot pan — colour equals flavour. Drain excess fat.
Add the onions and carrots; cook 10 minutes until sweet and soft.
Stir in the flour and tomato purée, then the stock, Marmite, bay and Worcestershire sauce. Simmer 25 minutes until rich and thick.
Mash the potatoes with butter and milk; season assertively.
Assemble in a baking dish, rough up the mash with a fork and scatter over the cheese if using.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 25 minutes until golden and bubbling.

title: Steak & Ale Pie
blurb: Slow-braised beef in a dark ale gravy beneath a buttery shortcrust lid — Britain’s most-ordered pub pie and the one every gastropub is judged by.
ingredients: 1 tbsp tomato purée; 1 tsp English mustard; 1 bay leaf
320g sheet all-butter shortcrust pastry; 1 egg, beaten
steps: Toss the beef in seasoned flour and brown in batches in hot dripping. Transfer to a casserole.
Soften the onions, carrots and mushrooms in the same pan for 8 minutes; add the tomato purée and mustard.
Pour in the ale, scraping up the browned bits, then the stock and bay. Return the beef.
Cover and braise at 160°C / 320°F (fan 140°C, gas 3) for 2 hours until the beef surrenders. Cool — a cold filling makes a crisper pie.
Tip the filling into a pie dish. Lay on the pastry, trim, crimp, cut a steam hole and glaze with egg.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 30–35 minutes until the crust is deep gold. Rest 10 minutes before serving with mash and greens.

title: Steak & Kidney Pie
blurb: The aristocrat of English pies — beef and ox kidney in a thick, peppery gravy under golden pastry. A pie that demands respect and a large appetite.
ingredients: 250g ox or lamb’s kidneys, trimmed and cubed
1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce; 1 tsp mustard powder
225g puff or shortcrust pastry; 1 egg, beaten
steps: Dust the steak and kidney with seasoned flour; brown in hot dripping in batches.
Soften the onions, then return the meat with the stock, stout, Worcestershire sauce and mustard powder.
Braise gently at 160°C / 320°F for 1½–2 hours until tender. Season and cool.
Fill a pie dish, set a pie funnel or upturned egg cup in the middle, and lid with pastry.
Crimp the edges, decorate with pastry leaves, glaze with egg and cut a vent.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 30–35 minutes until risen and golden. Serve with mash and peas.

title: Chicken & Mushroom Pie
blurb: Poached chicken and chestnut mushrooms folded through a tarragon cream sauce, lidded with shattering puff pastry — the nation’s favourite pie filling in poll after poll.
ingredients: 1 tbsp chopped tarragon or parsley; 1 tsp Dijon mustard
steps: Poach the chicken gently in the stock for 12 minutes; lift out and chop. Reserve the stock.
Fry the mushrooms and leek in butter for 8 minutes until golden at the edges.
Stir in the flour, cook 2 minutes, then whisk in the stock gradually until smooth and thick.
Off the heat, stir in the cream, mustard, tarragon and chicken. Season and cool.
Fill the pie dish, lid with puff pastry, crimp and glaze with egg.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is puffed and deeply golden.

title: The Cornish Pasty
blurb: Protected by European law and Cornish pride: beef skirt, potato, swede and onion crimped in a sturdy shortcrust — a complete meal for the tin miner’s hand.
ingredients: Pastry: 500g strong bread flour, 120g cold butter, 120g lard, 1 tsp salt, 175ml cold water
1 tbsp butter per pasty; salt and lots of black pepper
steps: Rub the fats into the flour and salt, bring together with cold water and knead until smooth. Rest 30 minutes.
Mix the raw beef, potato, swede and onion with aggressive seasoning — everything goes in raw.
Roll the pastry into 4 discs about 22cm across. Pile the filling on one half, dot with butter.
Fold over and crimp along the edge with a rope twist — the miner’s handle.
Glaze with egg, cut a small steam hole and bake at 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) for 45–50 minutes until deep golden.
Rest 10 minutes. Eat warm, out of the hand, ideally within sight of the sea.

title: Melton Mowbray Pork Pie
blurb: Hand-raised hot-water crust, uncured chopped pork, and a savoury jelly poured through the hole — the hunting-breakfast pie that defines an entire town.
ingredients: Hot-water crust: 450g strong flour, 100g lard, 150ml water, 1 tsp salt
Filling: 700g pork shoulder, coarsely chopped; 150g bacon, chopped
1 tsp each: salt, white pepper, mace; ½ tsp ground ginger; 2 tbsp chopped sage
Jelly: 300ml hot pork stock with 2 leaves gelatine
steps: Boil the lard and water, pour into the flour and salt, and mix to a smooth dough. Work it while warm.
Reserve a third for the lid. Raise the rest around a floured jam jar, working the dough up into a free-standing case.
Mix the pork, bacon and seasonings and pack firmly into the case.
Add the lid, crimp the edges, cut a central hole and glaze with egg.
Bake at 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) for 1½ hours, glazing again halfway, until deep amber.
When cooled to warm, funnel the gelatine stock through the hole in stages, letting it settle. Chill overnight before slicing — patience is the final ingredient.

title: Proper Fish Pie
blurb: Smoked haddock, cod and prawns in a parsley cream sauce beneath buttery mash — coastal England’s answer to the shepherd’s pie, and a Friday night institution.
ingredients: Sauce: 75g butter, 75g flour, the poaching milk, handful of chopped parsley
Topping: 1kg potatoes, 60g butter, splash of milk, 40g grated cheddar
steps: Poach the fish in the milk with bay and peppercorns for 5 minutes; lift out, flake, and strain the milk.
Make the sauce: melt the butter, stir in the flour for 2 minutes, whisk in the milk and simmer until thick. Add parsley.
Fold the flaked fish, prawns and eggs into the sauce and tip into a baking dish.
Mash the potatoes with butter and milk; spread over the filling, fork into waves and scatter with cheese.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 25–30 minutes until golden and bubbling at the edges.

title: Cheese & Onion Pie
blurb: Lancashire’s great vegetarian pie — sweet slow onions and sharp cheddar in shortcrust, born of ration-book ingenuity and still on every northern chippy counter.
ingredients: Shortcrust: 350g plain flour, 175g cold butter, pinch of salt, cold water
300g sharp Lancashire or mature cheddar, grated
steps: Make the pastry: rub the butter into the flour, bind with cold water, chill 30 minutes.
Melt the butter and sweat the onions very gently for 20 minutes until completely soft and sweet but not browned. Cool.
Fold the grated cheese through the onions with the egg, milk, salt and white pepper.
Line a 23cm pie plate with half the pastry, fill, and lid with the rest. Crimp and cut a vent.
Glaze with egg and bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 30–35 minutes until golden.
Rest 15 minutes before cutting — the filling sets as it stands. Serve with mushy peas and chips, naturally.

title: Steak & Kidney Pudding
blurb: England’s great steamed suet pudding — hours of gentle steaming produce a pale, tender crust around beef and kidney swimming in their own rich gravy.
ingredients: Suet crust: 350g self-raising flour, 175g shredded beef suet, 1 tsp salt, 200ml cold water
Filling: 700g braising steak, cubed; 200g ox kidney, cubed
300ml beef stock; 1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce; 1 tsp mustard
steps: Mix the flour, suet and salt; bind with cold water into a soft dough.
Roll out two-thirds and line a well-buttered 1.2-litre pudding basin.
Toss the steak and kidney in seasoned flour and pack into the basin with the onion.
Mix the stock, Worcestershire sauce and mustard; pour in to just below the rim.
Lid with the remaining pastry, pleat and seal. Cover with a pleated foil lid tied with string.
Steam over simmering water for 4 hours, topping up the pan — the crust should be pale and tender, never browned.
Turn out carefully and serve at the table, cutting the first slice so the gravy flows. Mashed potato and cabbage alongside.

title: Bangers & Mash with Onion Gravy
blurb: Our namesake and Britain’s most-loved pub plate: proper butcher’s sausages on cloud-soft mash, drowned in slow-caramelised onion gravy. “Bangers” for the way they burst in the pan — we cook them gently so they never do.
ingredients: Mash: 1kg Maris Piper potatoes, 75g butter, 100ml warm milk
Onion gravy: 3 onions, thinly sliced; 40g butter; 1 tsp sugar
1 tbsp flour; 500ml beef stock; 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar; sprig of thyme
steps: Start the gravy: melt the butter, add the onions and sugar, and cook gently for 20–25 minutes until deep amber. Rush this and you have onion stock, not gravy.
Meanwhile prick nothing — place the sausages in a frying pan with a splash of oil over medium-low heat and cook 15–20 minutes, turning, until evenly bronzed.
Boil the potatoes until very tender; drain, dry over the heat for a minute, and mash with butter and warm milk until silky.
Stir the flour into the onions, cook 1 minute, then add the stock, vinegar and thyme; simmer 5 minutes until glossy.
Serve a swoop of mash, three bangers standing proud, gravy over everything, peas on the side.

title: Fish & Chips
blurb: Britain’s national takeaway: cod in a crisp, singing batter with thick-cut chips, salt, vinegar and mushy peas. One of the few dishes spared wartime rationing — morale itself, fried.
ingredients: Batter: 150g plain flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 250ml very cold lager, pinch of salt
Chips: 800g Maris Piper potatoes, cut thick
Beef dripping or sunflower oil, for frying
Mushy peas, tartare sauce, lemon, malt vinegar — to serve
steps: Cut the chips and soak in cold water for 30 minutes; dry thoroughly.
Blanch the chips in oil at 130°C / 265°F for 6–8 minutes until soft but pale. Remove and rest.
Whisk the batter ingredients just before frying — lumps are fine, cold is essential.
Heat the oil to 180°C / 355°F. Dust the fish with flour, dip in the batter, and lower in gently.
Fry 6–8 minutes until deep gold and crisp; drain on a rack, not paper.
Refry the chips at 190°C / 375°F for 3–4 minutes until golden and crunchy.
Salt everything immediately, douse with malt vinegar, and serve with mushy peas and tartare sauce.

title: The Ploughman’s Lunch
blurb: A wedge of mature cheddar, crusty bread, pickled onions, chutney and an apple — the cold lunch that defined the British pub garden. No cooking, only standards.
ingredients: 300g mature farmhouse cheddar (or half cheddar, half Stilton)
Crusty white or granary bread; salted butter
1 crisp apple, quartered; handful of watercress
steps: Bring the cheese to room temperature — cold cheese is a wasted cheese.
Cut it into generous wedges, never cubes.
Arrange on boards with the bread, butter, pickles, chutney, apple and watercress.
Eat in the correct order: bread, butter, cheese, pickle. Repeat. Ale throughout.

title: Scotch Eggs
blurb: A soft-yolked egg wrapped in seasoned sausagemeat and fried to a deep amber — invented by Fortnum & Mason in 1738 and still the supreme picnic egg.
ingredients: 5 large eggs (4 for wrapping, 1 beaten for coating)
1 tbsp chopped sage; 1 tsp mustard powder; pinch of mace
steps: Soft-boil 4 eggs for exactly 6 minutes; chill in iced water and peel carefully.
Season the sausagemeat with sage, mustard powder and mace. Divide into 4 and wrap each egg in an even layer.
Flour, egg-wash and crumb each ball twice for a proper crust.
Deep-fry at 170°C / 340°F for 7–8 minutes until deep golden and cooked through.
Rest 5 minutes, cut to reveal the jammy yolk, and serve warm or cold with piccalilli.

title: Pie, Mash & Liquor
blurb: The Cockney sacrament: minced beef pies with mash and “liquor” — a vivid green parsley sauce that has nothing to do with alcohol and everything to do with the East End.
ingredients: Pies: 500g minced beef, 1 onion, 400ml beef stock, shortcrust base and suet or puff lid
Liquor: 25g butter, 25g flour, 500ml fish or light chicken stock
Large handful parsley, finely chopped; splash of malt vinegar
Chilli vinegar on the table, as is proper
steps: Simmer the mince and onion in the beef stock for 20 minutes; thicken with a flour slurry and season. Cool.
Fill pastry-lined pie tins, lid, crimp and bake at 200°C / 400°F for 25–30 minutes until golden.
For the liquor: make a white roux, whisk in the hot stock and simmer 5 minutes. Off the heat, add a mountain of parsley and a splash of vinegar — it should be unmistakably green.
Mash the potatoes softer than you think wise.
Serve pie and mash side by side, liquor ladled liberally over both, chilli vinegar to taste.

title: Chicken Tikka Masala
blurb: Officially “a true British national dish”: charred tikka chicken folded into a creamy tomato masala — the curry that out-sells roast dinners and tops UK recipe searches year after year.
ingredients: Tikka: 700g chicken thighs, 150g Greek yogurt, 2 tbsp tandoori masala, juice of ½ lemon
Sauce: 2 onions, 4 garlic cloves, 20g ginger, 2 tbsp butter and 1 tbsp oil
2 tbsp tomato purée; 1 tbsp garam masala; 1 tsp each cumin, coriander, smoked paprika
400g passata; 200ml double cream; 1 tsp sugar; fenugreek leaves if you can find them
Basmati rice and naan, to serve
steps: Marinate the chicken in the yogurt, tandoori masala and lemon for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight.
Grill the chicken at 240°C / 465°F for 12–15 minutes until charred at the edges. Rest.
Soften the onions in butter and oil for 15 minutes; add garlic, ginger and all the ground spices; cook 2 minutes.
Add the tomato purée and passata; simmer 10 minutes until brick-red and thick.
Blend smooth, return to the pan with the cream, sugar and fenugreek; simmer 5 minutes.
Fold in the chicken and its juices; simmer 5 minutes more. Serve over basmati rice with naan for scooping.

title: Beef in Ale Casserole
blurb: Slow-braised beef with carrots and pearl barley in dark ale — the sort of pot that has been bubbling beside inn fires for three centuries.
ingredients: 1 tbsp tomato purée; 2 bay leaves; few thyme sprigs
Horseradish dumplings, if you’re going properly to town
steps: Toss the beef in seasoned flour and brown in dripping in batches.
Soften the vegetables for 8 minutes; add the tomato purée, ale, stock, barley and herbs.
Cover and cook at 160°C / 320°F (fan 140°C, gas 3) for 2½ hours until the beef is spoon-tender.
Adjust the seasoning and consistency — it should be thick, dark and glossy.
Serve with mashed potato or suet dumplings and a glass of the same ale.

title: Hunter’s Chicken
blurb: Bacon-wrapped chicken baked in sticky barbecue sauce under a blanket of molten cheddar — the pub classic that has never once left Britain’s most-ordered list.
ingredients: Sauce: 150ml passata, 3 tbsp brown sugar, 2 tbsp cider vinegar, 1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp smoked paprika
steps: Wrap each chicken breast in two rashers of bacon; place in a baking dish.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 20 minutes.
Simmer the sauce ingredients together for 10 minutes until thick and glossy.
Pour the sauce over the chicken, blanket with cheddar and return to the oven for 12–15 minutes until the cheese is bubbling and bronzed.
Serve with chips, peas, and no pretension whatsoever.

title: Gammon, Egg & Chips
blurb: A thick gammon steak with a caramelised edge, a properly fried egg and a pile of chips — the pub grill’s eternal trio. Pineapple ring negotiable.
ingredients: 1 tsp English mustard; 1 tbsp brown sugar (for glazing)
Pineapple rings, optional; peas, to serve
steps: Snip the gammon rind in a few places so the steaks lie flat.
Blanch the chips at 130°C / 265°F for 6 minutes; drain and rest.
Mix the mustard and sugar; brush over the gammon. Grill or fry the steaks 4–5 minutes per side until caramelised.
Finish the chips at 190°C / 375°F for 4 minutes until golden.
Fry the eggs sunny-side up, slide onto the gammon, and serve with chips, peas and pineapple if the eighties mean anything to you.

title: Liver, Bacon & Onions
blurb: Calves’ liver flashed in the pan — never stewed — with crisp bacon, melting onions and proper gravy. The dish that converts liver sceptics, if it’s cooked right.
ingredients: 400g calves’ or lambs’ liver, sliced 1cm thick
steps: Fry the bacon until crisp; set aside. Soften the onions in the fat with the butter for 12 minutes until golden.
Add the flour to the onions, cook 1 minute, then add the stock and Worcestershire sauce; simmer into a light gravy.
Dust the liver with seasoned flour. In a separate screaming-hot pan, sear it in oil for 90 seconds per side — pink inside is correct.
Return the bacon to the onion gravy, warm through, and spoon over the liver with a mountain of mash.

title: Sausage & Bean Casserole
blurb: Browned sausages braised with beans, tomatoes and smoked paprika — the slow cooker’s most-searched British supper, four ingredients from a tin and proud of it.
ingredients: 400g tin cannellini or haricot beans, drained
250ml chicken stock; 1 tbsp tomato purée; 1 tsp smoked paprika
1 tsp dried mixed herbs; crusty bread, to serve
steps: Brown the sausages all over in a little oil; remove.
Soften the onion and garlic in the same pot for 8 minutes.
Add the tomato purée, paprika, tomatoes, stock, herbs and beans; return the sausages.
Simmer gently, half-covered, for 35–40 minutes until thick and rich — or transfer to a slow cooker on low for 6 hours.
Serve with crusty bread for dunking or a proper pile of mash.

title: Scampi & Chips
blurb: Sweet langoustine tails in golden breadcrumbs with chips, peas and tartare sauce — the great British pub seafood, unchanged and unimproved since 1974.
ingredients: 300g langoustine or large king prawn tails
800g potatoes for chips; oil for frying
Tartare sauce: 3 tbsp mayo, 1 tbsp chopped gherkins, 1 tsp capers, squeeze of lemon
Peas and lemon wedges, to serve
steps: Cut, soak and blanch the chips at 130°C / 265°F for 6 minutes; rest.
Flour, egg and crumb the scampi tails twice for a sturdy crust.
Deep-fry at 180°C / 355°F for 3–4 minutes until deep gold.
Refry the chips at 190°C / 375°F until crisp.
Serve with the tartare sauce, peas and lemon — ideally within earshot of a fruit machine.

title: Ham, Egg & Chips
blurb: Thick-cut carved ham, two fried eggs and proper chips — the transport-cafe Trinity, proof that three good things need no sauce at all.
ingredients: 2 thick slices carved cooked ham (about 200g each)
Butter for the eggs; malt vinegar and ketchup on the table
steps: Cut and soak the chips; blanch at 130°C / 265°F for 6 minutes and rest.
Warm the ham through under the grill for 3–4 minutes per side.
Refry the chips at 190°C / 375°F until golden and crisp.
Fry the eggs in butter until the whites are lacy and the yolks run.
Assemble in the only correct order: ham, eggs on top, chips alongside, vinegar on the chips.

title: Welsh Rarebit
blurb: The thinking person’s cheese on toast — a molten ale-and-mustard cheese sauce poured over toast and grilled until blistered. Add an egg and it becomes a buck rabbit.
ingredients: 1 tsp English mustard; few shakes Worcestershire sauce
A fried egg each, for buck rabbits (optional)
steps: Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook 1 minute.
Whisk in the ale to a smooth paste, then melt in the cheddar over a low heat — never let it boil.
Off the heat, beat in the mustard, Worcestershire sauce and yolk.
Spread thickly over the toast, right to the edges, and grill at 230°C / 450°F for 3–4 minutes until blistered and bronzed.
Crown with a fried egg for the full buck. Eat while molten.

title: Morecambe Bay Potted Shrimps
blurb: Tiny brown shrimps sealed beneath spiced, clarified butter — the taste of Morecambe Bay, served with hot toast for the butter to melt into.
ingredients: ¼ tsp ground mace; pinch of cayenne; ¼ tsp grated nutmeg
Juice of ½ lemon; salt and white pepper
steps: Melt the butter gently and let it settle; skim off the foam and pour off the clear butter, leaving the milky solids behind.
Warm the shrimps in the clarified butter with the mace, cayenne, nutmeg, lemon and seasoning for 2 minutes — do not cook them.
Pack into ramekins and seal with the remaining butter.
Chill until set, then bring back to cool room temperature before serving with hot toast.

title: Smoked Haddock with a Poached Egg
blurb: Undyed smoked haddock poached in milk, finished with butter and crowned with a poached egg — the grand hotel breakfast that never went out of fashion.
ingredients: Buttered spinach or toast, to serve
steps: Poach the haddock in the milk with the bay and peppercorns at a bare simmer for 6 minutes. Lift out and keep warm.
Meanwhile poach the eggs in barely simmering water with the vinegar for 3 minutes.
Serve the haddock on buttered spinach or toast, egg on top, with a knob of butter melting over everything.
A little of the poaching milk, reduced with cream, makes a fine impromptu sauce.

title: Dover Sole Meunière
blurb: The prince of flatfish, floured and fried in foaming butter with lemon and parsley — a dish of three ingredients and absolute precision.
ingredients: Juice of 1 lemon; 2 tbsp chopped parsley
New potatoes and green beans, to serve
steps: Pat the sole dry and dust lightly with seasoned flour, shaking off all excess.
Heat half the butter with the oil until foaming. Fry the sole 3–4 minutes per side until golden — turn once, carefully.
Remove the fish to warm plates. Wipe the pan.
Add the remaining butter and cook to a deep hazelnut brown; add the lemon juice — it will foam dramatically.
Pour the beurre noisette over the fish, scatter with parsley, and serve at once.

title: Salmon & Haddock Fishcakes
blurb: Flaked fish and buttery mash in a crisp golden crust — born of Victorian thrift, now the backbone of a thousand gastropub menus.
ingredients: Zest of 1 lemon; 2 tbsp chopped parsley and chives
Flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs for coating
Oil for frying; lemon wedges and peas, to serve
steps: Poach the fish in the milk for 5 minutes; drain, skin and flake into large pieces.
Fold the fish into the cold mash with the lemon zest, herbs, mustard and seasoning — keep the flakes chunky.
Shape into 8 cakes and chill 30 minutes to firm up.
Coat in flour, egg and breadcrumbs.
Shallow-fry in hot oil 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden and piping hot.
Serve with lemon wedges, buttered peas and tartare sauce.

title: Jellied Eels
blurb: The East End on a plate: poached eels set in their own savoury jelly, eaten cold with malt vinegar and white pepper beside a pie and mash shop counter.
ingredients: 800g fresh eels, skinned and cut into 5cm pieces
600ml fish stock; 1 onion, studded with 2 cloves; 1 bay leaf
1 tbsp white wine vinegar; squeeze of lemon
2 leaves gelatine (if the natural jelly needs help)
Malt vinegar, white pepper and chilli vinegar, to serve
steps: Simmer the stock with the onion, bay and vinegar for 10 minutes.
Poach the eel pieces gently for 12–15 minutes until the flesh flakes from the bone.
Lift the eels into a serving bowl. Strain the stock and reduce slightly; taste for seasoning and acidity.
If the stock isn’t naturally gelatine-rich, bloom and dissolve the gelatine leaves in it.
Pour the stock over the eels and chill overnight until softly set.
Serve cold with malt vinegar, a blizzard of white pepper, and no small amount of pride.

title: Cromer Dressed Crab
blurb: Sweet Cromer crab — brown meat enriched with yolk and mayonnaise, white meat left pure — arranged back in its shell with lemon and brown bread.
ingredients: 1 large cooked crab (about 1kg), or 300g picked mixed crabmeat
1 tsp lemon juice; dash of Worcestershire sauce
Cayenne, salt, white pepper; 1 tbsp fine breadcrumbs
Brown bread and butter, lemon wedges, cucumber — to serve
steps: Pick out the white meat from the claws and legs; keep it separate from the soft brown meat.
Mix the brown meat with the mayonnaise, mashed egg yolk, lemon juice, Worcestershire sauce, breadcrumbs and seasoning.
Spoon the brown mixture down the centre of the cleaned shell (or a serving dish).
Flank it with the flaked white meat on either side.
Serve simply with brown bread and butter, lemon and sliced cucumber.

title: Whitstable Oysters with Shallot Vinegar
blurb: Native Whitstable oysters eaten as the Romans found them — raw, cold, with nothing but a sharp mignonette of shallots and red wine vinegar.
ingredients: 6 fresh native oysters, alive and tightly closed
Cracked black pepper; crushed ice or rock salt, to serve
Lemon wedges; brown bread and butter
steps: Make the mignonette: steep the shallot in the vinegar with a good crack of pepper for 30 minutes.
Shuck the oysters over a bowl to catch every drop of liquor; cut them free and settle them back in the deep half-shell.
Nestle the shells on crushed ice or rock salt.
Serve with the mignonette, lemon and brown bread — and the discipline to add very little else.

title: Smoked Mackerel with Horseradish Cream
blurb: Peppered smoked mackerel with a fierce horseradish cream — oily fish, sharp heat, brown bread. The 15-minute starter that never misses.
ingredients: 4 smoked mackerel fillets, peppered if possible
150ml soured cream; 2–3 tbsp grated fresh horseradish (or creamed)
Squeeze of lemon; pinch of sugar; salt
Watercress; rye or brown bread, toasted
steps: Stir the soured cream with horseradish to your preferred ferocity, lemon juice, sugar and salt.
Skin the mackerel fillets and check for pin bones.
Arrange on plates with a tangle of watercress and the horseradish cream alongside.
Serve with hot toast and lemon wedges. Fifteen minutes, start to finish.

title: Leek & Potato Soup
blurb: Silky, pale and quietly perfect — leeks sweated long and slow in butter, blended with floury potatoes and finished with cream.
ingredients: 4 large leeks, sliced and well washed
1 litre light chicken or vegetable stock
steps: Sweat the leeks in butter under a lid for 15 minutes until completely soft — no colour.
Add the potatoes and stock; simmer 20 minutes until the potatoes collapse.
Blend until completely smooth, pass through a sieve if you’re being grand.
Stir in the cream, season with salt and white pepper, and serve with snipped chives.

title: Pea & Ham Soup
blurb: Split peas simmered to a velvet pottage with a ham hock’s smoky riches — London particular’s edible ancestor, built for the coldest days.
ingredients: White pepper; crusty bread, to serve
steps: Simmer the hock in the water for 1½ hours until the meat falls from the bone. Lift out; reserve the liquor.
Add the split peas, vegetables and bay to the liquor; simmer 45 minutes until the peas dissolve.
Shred the ham, discarding skin and bone.
Blend the soup to your preferred texture — half-smooth is the northern way.
Return the ham, warm through, season with white pepper, and serve with crusty bread.

title: Rich Oxtail Soup
blurb: Dark, glossy and deeply beefy — oxtails braised until they surrender into a soup once prescribed for invalids and now ordered purely for pleasure.
ingredients: 2 onions; 2 carrots; 2 celery sticks; 2 garlic cloves
2 tbsp tomato purée; 200ml red wine; 1.5 litres beef stock
2 bay leaves; few thyme sprigs; 1 tsp allspice berries
Splash of sherry, to finish; chopped parsley
steps: Flour and brown the oxtail in dripping in batches until deeply coloured.
Soften the vegetables, add the tomato purée and wine, and reduce by half.
Add the stock, herbs and allspice; braise gently for 3 hours.
Lift out the oxtail, shred the meat, and strain the broth. Skim the fat.
Return meat to broth, sharpen with sherry, and serve scattered with parsley.

title: Mulligatawny Soup
blurb: “Pepper-water” brought home from India and made our own — a curried chicken and rice soup sharpened with apple and lemon.
ingredients: 2 tbsp mild curry powder; 1 tbsp flour
Squeeze of lemon; chopped coriander; mango chutney, to serve
steps: Soften the onion, carrot and celery in butter for 10 minutes.
Add the apple, curry powder and flour; cook 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock, add the rice and chicken, and simmer 25 minutes.
Season, sharpen with lemon, and serve with coriander and a spoon of mango chutney.

title: The Prawn Cocktail
blurb: Cold sweet prawns in Marie Rose sauce over shredded lettuce — the starter that built a thousand Berni Inns and is once again, defiantly, cool.
ingredients: Marie Rose: 5 tbsp mayonnaise, 2 tbsp ketchup, dash of Worcestershire sauce, squeeze of lemon, splash of brandy (optional)
Buttered brown bread triangles, to serve
steps: Stir the sauce ingredients together and fold through the prawns.
Divide the lettuce between chilled glasses or coupes.
Spoon over the prawns and dust with cayenne.
Hang a few whole prawns over the rim, serve with brown bread triangles, and own the retro.

title: Chicken Liver Pâté
blurb: Silky, brandy-kissed pâté sealed under butter — the starter of a million 1970s dinner parties and still the best thing on toast before eight o’clock.
ingredients: 1 tsp thyme leaves; ¼ tsp ground allspice
Toast, cornichons and red onion marmalade, to serve
steps: Soften the shallot and garlic in 50g of butter for 5 minutes.
Turn up the heat, add the livers and sear 2–3 minutes — they must stay pink inside.
Add the brandy, thyme and allspice; flame or simmer 1 minute.
Blend with the remaining 100g butter until completely smooth; season assertively.
Pack into a terrine, seal with the melted butter and chill overnight.
Serve with hot toast, cornichons and marmalade.

title: Watercress Soup
blurb: Peppery Hampshire watercress whirled into a vivid green soup — the flavour of chalk streams and spring, ready in twenty minutes.
steps: Soften the onion in butter for 8 minutes. Add the potato and stock; simmer 12 minutes.
Add the watercress (reserve a few sprigs) and simmer just 2 minutes more to keep the colour.
Blend immediately until vivid green and smooth.
Swirl in the cream, season, and serve with the reserved sprigs floating on top.

title: Cream of Mushroom Soup
blurb: Field and chestnut mushrooms browned hard for depth, blended with cream and a whisper of garlic — everything the tinned version dreams of being.
ingredients: 900ml chicken or vegetable stock; 150ml double cream
Few drops of truffle oil or a grating of nutmeg, optional; chives
steps: Brown the mushrooms hard in batches in butter and oil — proper colour is where the flavour lives.
Add the onion and garlic; soften 5 minutes. Stir in the flour.
Add the stock gradually; simmer 15 minutes.
Blend most of the soup, leaving some mushrooms in slices for texture.
Finish with cream, season boldly, and serve with chives and hot buttered toast.

title: Perfect Roast Potatoes
blurb: Fluffy inside, shattering outside — the most-argued-over side dish in Britain, settled here with Maris Pipers, hot dripping and a good rattle of the colander.
ingredients: 1.5kg Maris Piper or King Edward potatoes, peeled, large chunks
4 tbsp beef dripping, goose fat or sunflower oil
Sea salt; few garlic cloves and rosemary (optional)
steps: Parboil the potatoes in well-salted water for 8 minutes until the edges soften.
Drain, steam dry 2 minutes, then rattle in the colander with the flour until the edges are roughed and furry.
Heat the fat in the roasting tin at 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7) until shimmering.
Add the potatoes — they should sizzle on contact. Turn to coat.
Roast 50–60 minutes, turning once, until deep gold and shattering.
Salt lavishly and serve immediately. Accept no leftovers; there won’t be any.

title: Cauliflower Cheese
blurb: Whole-baked cauliflower under a proper cheddar béchamel, bronzed and bubbling — the side dish that routinely upstages the roast itself.
ingredients: 1 large cauliflower, broken into large florets
Béchamel: 50g butter, 50g flour, 600ml milk, 1 tsp English mustard
150g mature cheddar, grated, plus 40g for the top
Pinch of nutmeg; salt and white pepper; 2 tbsp breadcrumbs
steps: Steam or boil the florets for 4–5 minutes until just tender; drain very well.
Make the béchamel: roux, then milk added gradually, simmered 3 minutes until thick.
Off the heat, stir in the mustard, nutmeg and cheddar. Season.
Combine in a baking dish, top with the extra cheese and breadcrumbs.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 20–25 minutes until burnished and bubbling.

title: Braised Red Cabbage with Apple
blurb: Slow-braised with Bramley apple, vinegar and spice — the sweet-sour purple anchor of every Christmas table and every good game dinner.
ingredients: 3 tbsp red wine vinegar; 2 tbsp soft brown sugar
¼ tsp each ground cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg; salt
steps: Layer everything into a heavy casserole with generous seasoning.
Dot with butter, lid on, and braise at 150°C / 300°F (fan 130°C, gas 2) for 1½–2 hours, stirring once or twice.
It should emerge silky, sweet-sour and deeply purple.
Serve with roast pork, goose or game — and note it improves made a day ahead.

title: Proper Mushy Peas
blurb: Marrowfat peas soaked overnight and simmered to a soft, savoury green mush — the non-negotiable third element of fish and chips north of the Trent.
steps: Soak the peas overnight in plenty of cold water with the bicarbonate of soda.
Drain, rinse, and cover with fresh water; simmer gently for 35–40 minutes, stirring, until collapsing into mush.
Beat in the butter and season — they should slump, not stand.
Serve beside fish and chips with malt vinegar, or under a pie in the northern fashion.

title: Bread Sauce
blurb: One of England’s oldest sauces — milk steeped with clove-studded onion, thickened with soft breadcrumbs and enriched with butter. Inseparable from roast chicken and turkey.
ingredients: 1 onion studded with 6 cloves; 2 bay leaves
steps: Bring the milk, clove-studded onion and bay to a bare simmer; infuse off the heat for 30 minutes.
Strain, return to the pan, and stir in the breadcrumbs.
Simmer gently 3–4 minutes until thick and porridgy.
Beat in the butter and cream; season with salt, white pepper and nutmeg. Serve warm.

title: Slow Onion Gravy
blurb: Onions caramelised for a patient half hour into a dark, glossy gravy — the only acceptable flood for bangers, mash, or toad in the hole.
ingredients: 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar; few thyme sprigs; splash of Worcestershire sauce
steps: Melt the butter, add the onions and sugar, and cook gently for 20–25 minutes, stirring, until deep amber throughout.
Stir in the flour and cook 1 minute.
Add the stock gradually, then the vinegar, thyme and Worcestershire sauce.
Simmer 5–8 minutes until glossy and coating. Season and serve in unwise quantities.

title: Honey-Roast Parsnips & Roots
blurb: Parsnips and carrots roasted hot in honey and mustard until burnished and candy-edged — the sweet counterweight in every Christmas and Sunday spread.
ingredients: 3 tbsp sunflower oil or goose fat
steps: Parboil the parsnips and carrots for 4 minutes; drain and steam dry.
Heat the oil in a roasting tin at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6).
Add the vegetables, season, and roast 30 minutes, turning once.
Whisk the honey and mustard, pour over, and roast 10–15 minutes more until glazed and caramelised.
Serve scattered with thyme — and guard them from early grazers.

title: Piccalilli
blurb: Crunchy vegetables in a fierce mustard-and-turmeric pickle — England’s yellow answer to chutney, essential beside pork pies, ploughman’s and cold ham.
ingredients: 1 small cauliflower, tiny florets; 2 onions, chopped; 200g green beans, sliced
2 tbsp mustard powder; 1 tbsp turmeric; 1 tbsp flour; 100g sugar
1 tbsp mustard seeds; 1 tsp ground ginger
steps: Brine the vegetables in salted water overnight; drain and rinse.
Simmer the vegetables in half the vinegar for 5 minutes — they must stay crunchy.
Mix the spices and flour to a paste with a little vinegar; add to the pan with the sugar and remaining vinegar.
Simmer 5 minutes until thickened and glossy.
Pack into hot sterilised jars, seal, and leave 2 weeks before attacking with cold meats and pork pies.

title: Victoria Sponge
blurb: Named for the Queen herself: two golden sponges, raspberry jam, softly whipped cream and a snowfall of caster sugar. The Women’s Institute standard against which all cakes are judged.
ingredients: 225g soft butter, plus extra for the tins
Filling: 5 tbsp raspberry jam; 200ml double cream, softly whipped
Caster or icing sugar, to dust
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4). Butter and line two 20cm sandwich tins.
Cream the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy — a full 5 minutes.
Beat in the eggs one at a time with a spoon of flour to prevent curdling.
Fold in the remaining flour and baking powder; loosen with the milk to a soft dropping consistency.
Divide between the tins and bake 22–25 minutes until golden and springing back.
Cool in the tins 5 minutes, then turn out and cool completely.
Sandwich with jam and cream, dust with sugar, and eat the same day — royalty doesn’t do leftovers.

title: Scones with Clotted Cream & Jam
blurb: The cream tea at the centre of Britain’s politest war: Devon says cream first, Cornwall says jam. We take no sides — only seconds.
ingredients: 350g self-raising flour, plus extra for dusting
175ml milk, plus 1 tbsp to glaze; 1 tsp lemon juice; 1 tsp vanilla (optional)
Clotted cream and strawberry jam, to serve
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7). Sift the flour and baking powder into a bowl.
Rub in the butter to fine crumbs; stir in the sugar.
Warm the milk slightly with the lemon juice, then cut it in with a knife to a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Pat out 4cm thick — never thinner. Cut rounds with a 6cm cutter, straight down, no twisting.
Glaze the tops only with milk and bake 10–12 minutes until risen and golden.
Split while warm and load with jam and clotted cream — in whichever order your conscience dictates.

title: Bakewell Tart
blurb: Born of a misunderstood order at the Rutland Arms: raspberry jam under a soft frangipane in crisp shortcrust — Derbyshire’s gift to the tea table.
ingredients: Shortcrust: 200g plain flour, 100g cold butter, 1 tbsp icing sugar, 1 egg yolk, cold water
Frangipane: 125g soft butter, 125g caster sugar, 2 eggs, 125g ground almonds, few drops almond extract
Flaked almonds, to scatter; icing sugar, to dust
steps: Make the pastry, line a 23cm tart tin and chill 30 minutes.
Blind-bake at 190°C / 375°F (fan 170°C, gas 5) for 12 minutes with beans, then 5 minutes without.
Spread the jam over the base.
Beat the frangipane ingredients together and spread over the jam. Scatter with flaked almonds.
Bake 30–35 minutes until golden and set with a slight wobble at the centre.
Dust with icing sugar and serve warm or cold, ideally with custard or cream.

title: Eccles Cakes
blurb: Flaky pastry parcels around buttery currants and brown sugar — sold in Eccles since 1793, banned by the Puritans, unstoppable ever since.
ingredients: Filling: 150g currants, 75g soft brown sugar, 50g melted butter, 1 tsp mixed spice, zest of 1 orange
1 egg white; demerara sugar, to finish
steps: Mix the currants, sugar, butter, spice and zest.
Roll the pastry to 3mm and cut 12cm rounds.
Pile a spoonful of filling in the centre of each; draw up the edges and seal.
Turn seam-side down and flatten gently until the currants just show through.
Cut three slashes, brush with egg white and dredge with demerara.
Bake at 220°C / 425°F (fan 200°C, gas 7) for 15–18 minutes until puffed and golden. Eat warm, with Lancashire cheese if you know what’s good for you.

title: Chelsea Buns
blurb: Sticky, glazed spirals of fruit and spice from the old Bun House on Pimlico Road — once so popular that George III queued for them.
ingredients: Dough: 300g strong bread flour, 1 tsp salt, 7g yeast, 150ml warm milk, 1 egg, 40g butter, 30g sugar
Filling: 75g soft butter, 75g soft brown sugar, 150g mixed dried fruit, 2 tsp mixed spice
Glaze: 2 tbsp milk and 2 tbsp caster sugar, warmed together
steps: Knead the dough ingredients for 8 minutes; prove 1 hour until doubled.
Roll into a 30×23cm rectangle. Spread with butter, sugar, fruit and spice.
Roll up tightly from the long edge; cut into 9 slices.
Pack into a lined 23cm square tin, prove 30 minutes.
Bake at 190°C / 375°F (fan 170°C, gas 5) for 18–20 minutes until golden.
Brush with the glaze while hot. Tear apart and eat warm, sticky fingers mandatory.

title: Simnel Cake
blurb: The Easter fruit cake with a marzipan heart and eleven marzipan apostles on top — served since medieval Mothering Sunday.
ingredients: 175g plain flour; ½ tsp each cinnamon and mixed spice
500g mixed dried fruit; zest of 1 lemon; 2 tbsp brandy or milk
500g marzipan, divided; 1 tbsp apricot jam, warmed
steps: Cream the butter and sugar; beat in the eggs; fold in the flour, spices, fruit and zest.
Line a deep 18cm tin. Add half the batter.
Roll a third of the marzipan into an 18cm disc and lay it in the middle. Add the remaining batter.
Bake at 150°C / 300°F (fan 130°C, gas 2) for 1 hour 45 minutes until a skewer comes out clean. Cool.
Top with another marzipan disc, crimp the edges, and ball the rest into 11 apostles.
Brush with egg and grill or torch briefly to toast the marzipan. Serve at Easter with tea.

title: Battenberg Cake
blurb: The pink-and-yellow chequerboard wrapped in marzipan — created for a royal wedding in 1884 and still the most architecturally satisfying slice on any cake stand.
ingredients: 175g self-raising flour; 50g ground almonds; few drops almond extract
4 tbsp apricot jam, warmed and sieved
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4). Line a 20cm square tin with a foil divider down the middle.
Beat everything except the colouring to a smooth batter.
Colour half the batter pink; fill the two halves of the tin separately.
Bake 22–25 minutes until risen and springy. Cool completely.
Trim the sponges and cut each into two long rectangles.
Assemble in chequerboard fashion, brushing jam between the strips.
Roll the marzipan into a rectangle, wrap the cake tightly with the seam underneath, and crimp the top edges. Slice to serve.

title: Lemon Drizzle Cake
blurb: Year after year among Britain’s most-baked and most-searched cakes — a soft lemon sponge impregnated with a crackling citrus syrup.
ingredients: Drizzle: juice of 2 lemons, 85g caster sugar
Icing (optional): 100g icing sugar, 2 tbsp lemon juice
steps: Heat the oven to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4); line a 900g loaf tin.
Beat the butter, sugar and zest until pale; add the eggs one by one, then fold in the flour.
Bake 45–50 minutes until golden and a skewer comes out clean.
While hot, stab all over with a skewer and slowly spoon over the lemon juice and sugar.
Cool in the tin so every drop of syrup is absorbed. Ice if you like, slice thickly, watch it vanish.

title: Yorkshire Parkin
blurb: Sticky, dark ginger-and-oat cake that improves with a week in the tin — the edible essence of Bonfire Night in God’s own county.
ingredients: 200g butter; 200g golden syrup; 100g black treacle; 120g soft dark sugar
1 tbsp ground ginger; 1 tsp mixed spice
steps: Melt the butter, syrups and sugar together gently; cool slightly.
Mix the flour, oatmeal and spices; beat in the syrup mixture, then the eggs and milk.
Pour into a lined 20cm square tin.
Bake at 150°C / 300°F (fan 130°C, gas 2) for 50–60 minutes until firm to the touch.
The hard part: wrap and leave in the tin for 3–7 days to turn properly sticky. Serve in squares by firelight.

title: Egg Custard Tart
blurb: Silky nutmeg-dusted custard wobbling in crisp pastry — the bakery-counter classic that England has loved since the court of Richard III.
ingredients: Shortcrust: 225g plain flour, 110g cold butter, 1 tbsp icing sugar, 1 egg yolk, cold water
Custard: 300ml whole milk, 150ml double cream, 4 egg yolks, 60g caster sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
steps: Line a 20cm flan tin with the pastry; chill 30 minutes.
Blind-bake at 180°C / 350°F for 15 minutes with beans, 5 without. Reduce the oven to 140°C / 285°F (fan 120°C, gas 1).
Warm the milk and cream. Whisk the yolks and sugar; pour on the warm milk, whisking.
Strain into the pastry case and grate nutmeg generously over the top.
Bake 30–35 minutes until just set with a gentle wobble at the centre.
Cool completely before slicing — the custard finishes setting as it stands.

title: Dorset Apple Cake
blurb: A sturdy, apple-crowded cake from cider country — served warm with clotted cream after a walk, as is the law in Dorset tearooms.
ingredients: 225g self-raising flour; 2 tsp baking powder; 1 tsp mixed spice
2 Bramley or sharp eating apples, peeled and diced
2 tbsp demerara sugar, to finish; clotted cream, to serve
steps: Cream the butter and sugar; beat in the eggs; fold in the flour, baking powder and spice.
Fold in the diced apple — the batter will be thick with fruit, which is the point.
Spread into a lined 20cm tin, scatter with demerara.
Bake at 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) for 50–55 minutes until golden and set.
Serve warm in generous slabs with clotted cream melting over the top.

title: Lardy Cake
blurb: A Wiltshire bakery legend — enriched dough layered with lard, sugar and fruit, baked until the bottom becomes a caramel. Not for the faint-hearted; entirely for the happy.
ingredients: Dough: 450g strong bread flour, 1 tsp salt, 7g yeast, 250ml warm milk, 50g lard
Layering: 175g lard, 175g soft brown sugar, 200g mixed dried fruit, 1 tsp mixed spice
Glaze: 2 tbsp sugar dissolved in 2 tbsp boiling water
steps: Knead the dough 8 minutes; prove 1 hour.
Roll into a rectangle. Dot with a third of the lard, sugar, fruit and spice; fold in thirds. Repeat twice more.
Press into a lined 23cm square tin; prove 30 minutes. Score the top in a criss-cross.
Bake at 200°C / 400°F (fan 180°C, gas 6) for 35–40 minutes until deep golden.
Glaze while hot, cool 10 minutes, then turn out — the sugary base becomes the top. Serve in squares, slightly warm.

title: Manchester Tart
blurb: Jam, custard, coconut and a cherry in crisp pastry — the school-dinner tart that Mancunians defend with the same passion as their football clubs.
ingredients: Shortcrust: 200g plain flour, 100g cold butter, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 egg yolk, cold water
5 tbsp raspberry jam; 1 sliced banana (optional, controversial)
Custard: 400ml milk, 3 yolks, 50g sugar, 2 tbsp custard powder, 1 tsp vanilla
steps: Line a 23cm tart tin with pastry; chill, then blind-bake at 190°C / 375°F for 15 minutes. Cool.
Spread the jam over the base (and banana, if you’re that sort of traditionalist).
Make a thick custard: whisk the yolks, sugar and custard powder with the warm milk and vanilla until very thick.
Pour over the jam and chill until set.
Shower with coconut, dot with cherries, and serve in wedges.

title: Sticky Toffee Pudding
blurb: Britain’s most-ordered restaurant pudding: a dark, date-soft sponge flooded with hot toffee sauce. Invented in the Lake District, beloved everywhere custard is poured.
ingredients: 200g stoned dates, chopped; 300ml boiling water; 1 tsp bicarbonate of soda
85g soft butter; 175g soft dark sugar; 2 eggs
Sauce: 175g soft dark sugar, 50g butter, 200ml double cream, pinch of salt
Custard, cream or vanilla ice cream, to serve
steps: Soak the dates in the boiling water with the bicarbonate for 15 minutes.
Cream the butter and sugar; beat in the eggs and vanilla; fold in the flour, then the dates and their liquid.
Bake in a lined 20cm square tin at 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) for 30–35 minutes until springy.
Simmer the sauce ingredients together for 5 minutes until glossy.
Stab the pudding all over, pour over half the sauce, and serve in squares with the rest of the sauce and custard. No restraint is expected.

title: Spotted Dick with Custard
blurb: The steamed suet pudding with the schoolboy-famous name — currant-spotted, lemon-scented, and impossible to serve without custard and a straight face.
ingredients: 100g caster sugar; 150g currants; zest of 1 lemon
Proper custard: 500ml milk, 4 yolks, 50g sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
steps: Mix the flour, suet, sugar, currants, zest and salt; bind with the milk to a soft dough.
Shape into a log and wrap loosely in buttered, pleated foil.
Steam over simmering water for 1½ hours until firm and well-risen.
Meanwhile make the custard: warm the milk, whisk into the yolks and sugar, and stir over low heat until it coats the spoon.
Slice the pudding thickly and drown in custard.

title: Bread & Butter Pudding
blurb: Buttered bread layered with sultanas and baked in nutmeg custard until the top crisps — thrift turned into one of the most comforting puddings in the canon.
ingredients: Custard: 500ml whole milk, 100ml double cream, 3 eggs, 75g caster sugar, 1 tsp vanilla
Extra custard or cream, to serve
steps: Cut the buttered bread into triangles and layer in a buttered baking dish, scattering sultanas between the layers.
Whisk the custard ingredients and pour over; press the bread down gently and rest 30 minutes to soak.
Grate over nutmeg and scatter with demerara.
Bake at 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4) for 35–40 minutes until puffed, golden and just set.
Rest 10 minutes, then serve with yet more custard. This is not the time for restraint.

title: Eton Mess
blurb: Strawberries, cream and crushed meringue — the gloriously chaotic pudding of the Eton–Harrow cricket match, at its absolute best in high summer.
ingredients: 1 tbsp icing sugar; squeeze of lemon
A few extra strawberries and mint, to finish
steps: Macerate half the strawberries with the sugar and lemon for 15 minutes, then crush roughly into a sauce.
Whip the cream with the vanilla to soft peaks.
Break the meringue into large, craggy pieces.
Fold the meringue, remaining strawberries and most of the sauce through the cream — marble, don’t mix.
Pile into glasses, ripple with the last of the sauce, and serve within the hour while the meringue still crackles.

title: Proper English Trifle
blurb: Sherry-soaked sponge, fruit, custard and cream in a glass bowl — the towering architecture of every British celebration since your grandmother’s grandmother.
ingredients: 1 trifle sponge or Madeira cake, sliced
4 tbsp raspberry jam; 400g raspberries (or tinned fruit, for the purists’ controversy)
Custard: 600ml milk, 5 yolks, 60g sugar, 1 tbsp cornflour, 1 tsp vanilla
300ml double cream, whipped; flaked almonds and a cherry, to finish
steps: Spread the sponge with jam, layer into the bowl and soak evenly with sherry. Rest 30 minutes.
Scatter over the fruit.
Make a proper pouring custard, cool it with a cartouche to prevent a skin, then pour over the fruit. Chill until set.
Pile on the whipped cream in billows.
Finish with toasted almonds and the cherry. Chill 4 hours — a trifle must know itself before serving.

title: Treacle Tart
blurb: Golden syrup, breadcrumbs and lemon in crisp shortcrust — Harry Potter’s favourite and Britain’s stickiest slice, served warm with cream.
ingredients: Shortcrust: 200g plain flour, 100g cold butter, 1 tbsp icing sugar, 1 egg yolk, cold water
Filling: 450g golden syrup, 100g fresh white breadcrumbs, zest and juice of 1 lemon, 1 egg
Double cream or custard, to serve
steps: Line a 23cm tart tin with pastry; chill 30 minutes.
Blind-bake at 190°C / 375°F for 12 minutes with beans, 5 without. Reduce to 180°C / 350°F (fan 160°C, gas 4).
Warm the syrup until runny; stir in the breadcrumbs, lemon zest, juice and egg.
Pour into the case — lattice the top with pastry trimmings if you’re feeling fancy.
Bake 25–30 minutes until just set and deep gold.
Serve warm with cold cream, and accept that seconds are inevitable.

title: Jam Roly-Poly
blurb: Suet pastry rolled around raspberry jam and steamed until pillowy — the school-dinner legend known affectionately everywhere as “dead man’s arm”.
ingredients: 250g self-raising flour; 125g shredded suet; pinch of salt
steps: Mix the flour, suet and salt; bind with water to a soft dough.
Roll into a 20×28cm rectangle; spread with jam, leaving a border.
Roll up from the short side like a Swiss roll.
Wrap loosely in buttered, pleated foil, sealing the ends.
Steam for 1½ hours until well risen and cooked through.
Slice into thick spirals and serve with an irresponsible amount of custard.

title: Apple Crumble
blurb: Britain’s most-baked pudding — born when rationing killed the pie, perfected by every family since. Bramleys beneath a rubble of butter, flour and sugar.
ingredients: 2 tbsp caster sugar; splash of water; ½ tsp cinnamon
Crumble: 180g plain flour, 120g cold butter, 90g demerara sugar, pinch of salt
Custard, cream or ice cream, to serve
steps: Simmer the apples with the sugar, water and cinnamon for 5 minutes until just starting to slump. Tip into a baking dish.
Rub the butter into the flour and salt until it resembles rough breadcrumbs; stir in the sugar.
Scatter the crumble loosely over the fruit — never press it down.
Bake at 190°C / 375°F (fan 170°C, gas 5) for 35–40 minutes until the top is golden and the juices bubble up at the edges.
Serve with custard, and brook no argument about it.

title: Banoffee Pie
blurb: Invented in Sussex in 1971 and now a global classic: biscuit base, caramelised condensed milk, bananas and coffee-kissed cream.
ingredients: 397g tin caramel (or condensed milk boiled for 3 hours, the old way)
1 tsp instant coffee dissolved in 1 tbsp hot water (optional)
steps: Crush the biscuits, mix with the butter and press firmly into a 23cm fluted tin. Chill 30 minutes.
Spread the caramel over the base.
Layer the bananas over the caramel.
Whip the cream (with coffee if using) to soft peaks and pile on top.
Grate over dark chocolate and chill 1 hour before slicing.

title: Old-Fashioned Baked Rice Pudding
blurb: Short-grain rice baked long and slow in sweetened milk under a burnished nutmeg skin — the nursery pudding that divides families over whether the skin is the best bit. (It is.)
ingredients: 1 tsp vanilla or a strip of lemon peel
Jam or stewed fruit, to serve
steps: Butter a baking dish; add the rice, sugar and milk and stir.
Add the vanilla, dot with butter and grate over nutmeg generously.
Bake at 150°C / 300°F (fan 130°C, gas 2) for 2–2½ hours, stirring twice in the first hour.
It’s ready when creamy beneath and deeply bronzed on top.
Serve warm with a spoon of jam melting into it.

title: Summer Pudding
blurb: White bread soaked through with the juice of summer berries until it turns the colour of a garnet — the great no-bake pudding of the English summer.
ingredients: 800g mixed summer berries (raspberries, redcurrants, blackcurrants, blackberries)
8–10 slices day-old white bread, crusts removed
steps: Simmer the berries with the sugar and water for 5 minutes until the juices run; cool slightly.
Line a 1-litre pudding basin with the bread, cutting to fit snugly with no gaps.
Fill with the fruit and most of the juice; lid with more bread.
Weight down with a plate and a tin; chill overnight.
Turn out — it should gleam garnet-red — and serve with the reserved juice and clotted cream.

title: Christmas Pudding
blurb: Made on Stir-up Sunday, steamed for hours, aged for weeks, and carried to the table in flames — the most ceremonial dish in the English year.
ingredients: 400g mixed dried fruit; 100g glacé cherries; 50g chopped almonds
100ml brandy or stout, plus more for feeding; zest of 1 orange and 1 lemon
110g shredded suet; 110g fresh breadcrumbs; 110g plain flour; 175g soft dark sugar
1 tsp mixed spice; ½ tsp grated nutmeg; 1 apple, grated; 2 eggs
Brandy butter: 100g soft butter, 100g icing sugar, 3 tbsp brandy
steps: Soak the fruit in the brandy overnight. Stir in everything else — clockwise, with a wish, as tradition demands.
Pack into a buttered 1.2-litre basin; cover with pleated parchment and foil, tied with string.
Steam for 6 hours, topping up the water regularly.
Cool, re-wrap and store in a cool dark place for up to 6 weeks, feeding with brandy fortnightly.
On the day: steam 2 hours more to reheat.
Warm a ladle of brandy, set it alight, and pour it flaming over the pudding. Serve with hard brandy butter that melts into glory.
